LLC is an EXEMPT REPORTING ADVISER (SEC 802-75842, CRD 160352, ERA since 2012-03-30), not a registered investment adviser, so no Item 5.F regulatory AUM exists. The sworn substitute is Schedule D Section 7.B.(1): 34 private funds whose current gross asset values sum to $7,582,538,663 on the annual amendment filed 2026-03-24 (parsed at run time by scratch/own-formd-persons.py's sibling ADV pass). funds.basis: The flagship ladder plus the two 2026 vehicles and the Cerebras pair. FILING STYLE MATTERS HERE and it is the opposite of Lightspeed's: Benchmark files the FULL fund size as the Form D total-offering amount at or before first close, so the offering is the fund size and the sold amount is the close state on the filing date — Fund VII shows $5M sold against a $425M offering, Fund IX $0 against $425M. Sizes are therefore the offering amounts, asserted against the accessions. Funds I, II, IV, V and VI (1995-2008) predate electronic Form D and carry no sworn size; the firm held every flagship at roughly $425M from 2011 to 2024. The 18 Founders' Fund co-invest vehicles, the Management Co. GPs and the WS SPV are counted in the base's evidence but not listed as funds — they are employee co-invest and GP plumbing, not capital raised from LPs.

history.value: Benchmark was founded in Menlo Park in 1995 by Bob Kagle, Bruce Dunlevie, Andy Rachleff, Kevin Harvey and Val Vaden, and built its reputation on an equal partnership with no junior or senior partners, no CEO and no name on the door. Bob Kagle's $6.7 million Series A into eBay in 1997 for about 22% became the best-performing venture investment in Silicon Valley history, and the same first-institutional-round pattern produced Juniper Networks, Red Hat, Equinix and Handspring before 2000, then Yelp, Zillow, OpenTable, Zuora, New Relic and Asana, then Bill Gurley's $11 million Series A into Uber in 2011, Matt Cohler's $7 million into Instagram the same year, Mitch Lasky's $13.5 million into Snapchat in 2013 and Peter Fenton's $10 million into Elasticsearch in 2012. The firm ran a London desk from 2000 and an Israeli desk from 2001; both became separate firms, Balderton Capital in 2007 and Benchmark Israel VC 2007 Ltd, and their portfolios are not counted here. Benchmark held its funds at roughly $425 million for two decades, and broke that discipline in 2026: two vehicles raised in February to put about $225 million into a single Cerebras round, and $2 billion in June across a $750 million early-stage fund and Benchmark Partners T1, at $1.25 billion the firm's first dedicated growth fund. It manages 34 private funds holding $7.58 billion, and publishes no portfolio list at all; its website has been a single page with two addresses since 2013. The 284 companies recorded here run from 1995 to 2026 and are overwhelmingly Series A entries, with 24 at $1 billion or more.
history.basis: Assembled from the sources cited across this sidecar plus the run's own evidence: the fund ladder from Form D, the desk history from the archived site and the 2007 Balderton and Benchmark Israel VC 2007 separations, the 2026 fund raises from TechCrunch (2026-02-06 and 2026-06-03), and the base's own shape.

investment_concept.value: Benchmark backs founders at the first institutional round and takes a board seat, one equal partnership, one fund at a time.
investment_concept.basis: DERIVED — the firm publishes no thesis, no positioning statement and no marketing copy of any kind; its entire website is a wordmark and two addresses. The sentence is assembled from what the record actually establishes: the equal-partnership structure the firm has described in interviews (no junior or senior partners, no CEO, profits driven by investment performance rather than management fees), the first-institutional-round-plus-board-seat pattern that 243 of 284 base rows are Series A entries evidences directly, and the one-fund-at-a-time discipline visible in the fund ladder (roughly $425M per flagship from 2011 to 2024). It is a description, not a quotation.
